final.title: When glossary upkeep should stay manual
final.body:
If glossary upkeep is starting to feel like its own little job, the first question is simple: is it frequent, repeatable, and tied to a measurable outcome, or is it just occasional cleanup?

For a 1–10 person business, that distinction matters. If glossary edits are rare and mostly one-off judgment calls, automation is probably a distraction. If the work keeps coming back in the same pattern, it may be a bounded workflow worth testing.

The next step is not to automate the whole glossary. Write down one recurring rule in plain English, such as: when does a term need a new definition, when does a correction need owner sign-off, and what should never change without review?

That keeps the human decision where it belongs and makes the workflow easier to judge. Bareni’s current boundary is the same one we use elsewhere: human approval stays in place for high-risk decisions, and paper-heavy or OCR-dependent work is out of scope.

If the rule is still hard to state clearly, that is usually the answer. The glossary is not the problem; the process is.

final.title: When glossary upkeep becomes overhead
final.body:
Glossary upkeep stops being useful when it no longer helps the same people answer the same operational question the same way.

If you run a small business, the check is simple: does the glossary reduce repeat questions, or has it turned into another document you now have to maintain?

That matters because not every recurring task deserves automation. Some work is frequent and repeatable. Some is just admin wearing better shoes.

A practical next step is to review the last week of repeated questions or term fixes and sort them into three buckets: keep as-is, merge into another workflow, or retire. If a term only needs a human judgment call once in a while, glossary upkeep may be the wrong place to spend attention. If it keeps changing how people answer customers, it still has a job.

For Bareni, that is the kind of bounded decision we look at: one recurring workflow, one clear rule, and human approval where the owner wants it. If the source material is paper-heavy or OCR-dependent, that is outside current scope and needs a different answer.
